newsitem.title: THAILAND: Philippines sees no peso depreciation, minister.
newsitem.headline: Philippines sees no peso depreciation, minister.

text.p: Philippines Finance Minister Roberto de Ocampo said on Saturday the Philippines had no plan to depreciate the peso to help boost exports and would leave the currency to fluctuate according to market forces.

De Ocampo told Reuters the Philippine economy was in good shape and the country expected Moody's Investors Service Inc to follow a recent move by Standard and Poor's Corp to upgrade its credit ratings.
The Philippine peso has largely held steady against the U.S. dollar as the U.S. unit has strengthened over the past 12 months, leading to its appreciation against other major currencies.
He said: "We're allowing the peso to move in accordance with market forces. We are not persuaded there is any need to change tact."

"Usually those indicating the need to change seem to be espousing the idea of an arbitrary move designed...to enhance export competitiveness but time and time again in the past, we have had experience of using the people's wisdom, rather than the wisdom of the market place, and getting ourselves burned. We are going to stick to our guns right now," the minister said.
He said S&P's decision in February to upgrade Philippine long-term foreign currency debt rating to BB-plus from BB would likely prompt Moody's and other credit rating agencies to follow suit.

"They usually follow one another in rapid succession. Market analysts have been looking at the credit rating of the Philippines and tend to make a persuasive case that we are underrated even after the S&P upgrade," he said.
De Ocampo said Philippine private borrowers would be the main beneficiaries of the country's improving rating when they entered international bond markets.

He said the Philippine government has no plan to tap fresh foreign commercial loans at least during the first nine months of 1997 while its central bank plans to raise between $750- million and $1.0 billion through 30-year/100-year Yankee bonds soon, mainly to help establish bond coupon benchmarks.
